trace: The prompt asks me to attribute a low-volatility momentum strategy's deterioration from a 15-year Sharpe of 1.10 down to 0.35 over the last three years. The strategy blends two distinct factor premia — momentum (UMD) and low-volatility (BAB/betting-against-beta) — selecting 75 stocks by 6-month risk-adjusted performance and rebalancing quarterly. My first instinct is to separate the structural logic from the cyclical headwinds. Historically, combining momentum with a volatility filter makes sense: it removes the junk side of momentum, where cheap, volatile names can distort returns. That hybrid explains the 1.10 Sharpe, which is genuinely strong for a 15-year period. Now for the deterioration. Three channels strike me as most plausible. First, the correlation between momentum and low-volatility has historically fluctuated; when it breaks down, the portfolio loses its internal hedge. In recent years — particularly post-2022 — we saw sharp factor rotations where high-beta and previously beaten-down cyclicals surged, which punished both factors simultaneously rather than letting one offset the other. Second, the rate environment matters enormously. Low-volatility stocks carry an implicit duration, behaving like bond proxies. With the Fed hiking 525 basis points between March 2022 and mid-2023, those holdings saw a structural revaluation drag — the completion estimates a -15% contribution from this channel, which seems directionally correct. Third, quarterly rebalancing creates a roughly 45-day average signal lag; in a fast-rotating market that is genuinely punitive, as yesterday's risk-adjusted winners become tomorrow's laggards within weeks rather than quarters. The attribution ascribes about -18% contribution from momentum crowding, which I find credible given AQR and similar shops all holding similar names. The alpha's t-stat of 2.95 over the full period is meaningful, but I want to see whether it survives the last three years in isolation — the Sharpe collapse to 0.35 implies it likely does not. The recommended fixes — dynamic signal blending, rate sensitivity hedging, adaptive rebalancing — address the real problems rather than cosmetically tweaking parameters. I weight the regime shift as the primary cause rather than any single mechanical flaw.

This is a classic deep value attribution: bottom 50 P/B from the Russell 1000, quarterly rebalanced, Sharpe 0.85 over 15 years but with a -58% max drawdown at GFC and a -35% drawdown across 2018-2020. The core tension here is between the statistical significance of the value premium and its cyclical brutality. The 15-year result is real — the HML factor captures a genuine if lumpy risk premium — but the alpha after factor adjustment is only 0.45% annualized with a t-stat of 0.91 and a p-value of 0.36. That means almost everything is factor exposure, not stock-picking. Walk-forward validation shows a 35% Sharpe decay, which is the honest fingerprint of factor cyclicality rather than overfitting, since the strategy is parameter-light. The sector concentration issue is key and often under-discussed: persistent +18% overweight to Financials and +9% to Energy explains most of the large drawdowns. These sectors aren't random; they're structurally cheap on P/B because they're capital-intensive and have poor intangible assets, but they're also cyclically leveraged. The five-year value drought (2017-2021) was regime-driven, not a fluke. I have high conviction that the -3.1% annualized HML contribution in the recent period is the primary cause — the sector bets and the missing quality filter are compounding secondary issues. The recommendations to add a quality screen (ROE filter), sector neutralize, and overlay a momentum exclusion for falling knives all target real structural deficiencies. Switching from P/B alone to a composite including P/FCF and EV/EBITDA deserves emphasis since P/B systematically misprices intangible-heavy businesses. This is a serviceable factor vehicle that needs modernization, not abandonment.

A concentrated momentum strategy — top 30 names by 9-month price return, quarterly rebalanced — showing a Sharpe collapse from 0.90 to 0.20 over the last three years. The 15-year figure is anchored heavily on the UMD factor, which the attribution puts at a 0.78 beta explaining 55% of variance. That is high single-factor dependence, which means any momentum drawdown hits hard. The true alpha after factor adjustment is only 1.2% annually with a t-stat of 2.1, modest but significant. My main concern is the quarterly rebalancing combined with a short concentrated portfolio. Thirty stocks creates high idiosyncratic risk; if three or four names blow up during a sharp rotation, the portfolio has little buffer. The 9-month lookback is in the canonical momentum sweet spot historically, but the completion's own walk-forward analysis flags a 45% Sharpe decay and high sensitivity to the lookback parameter — a 1-month shift changes the Sharpe by 0.11 on average, which is a red flag for overfitting to historical momentum cycles. The recent deterioration maps to the 2022-2023 period, when momentum crashed repeatedly: first growth stocks dropped, then energy surged, then tech recovered — all within compressed timeframes that a quarterly rebalance cannot track. The Sharpe of -0.35 during reversal periods versus 1.45 in trending markets tells the whole story. Transaction costs matter here too: the strategy has 85% annual turnover and the backtest uses 10 bps per one-way transaction, which is probably optimistic. Recommendations to shift to a risk-adjusted momentum signal and increase portfolio size to 50+ stocks address the right problems. The regime-awareness overlay is the highest-value addition I would prioritize.

The Defensive Value strategy combines two screens — low Price-to-Book and low 12-month realized volatility — and achieved a 10-year Sharpe of 0.95 while still suffering a -35% drawdown in March 2020. That combination is the central puzzle. In theory, low-vol should provide a buffer; in practice, the two-step sequential screening created a path-dependent concentration that the attribution rightly flags. First selecting for cheap P/B stocks and then filtering for low-vol within that already-distressed universe systematically loaded the portfolio into Financials and Industrials — sectors that had appeared stable on trailing vol metrics right up until the COVID shock. When volatility spiked from VIX 12 to VIX 82 in six weeks, the trailing 12-month lookback was completely blind to emerging risk. The attribution correctly identifies that 78% of returns come from the dual Value and Low-Volatility factor exposures, with a statistically insignificant residual alpha (t-stat 0.8). That means the strategy is a factor-carry vehicle, not a stock-picking machine. The regime vulnerability is acute: +4.2% annualized alpha in range-bound markets, catastrophic failure in dislocations. The recommendation to add a quality screen — profitability, low accruals — addresses the value-trap problem directly. The VIX-based leverage scaling is the right instrument for the COVID-style shock: reduce gross exposure as implied vol spikes. Moving to a composite factor score rather than sequential screens would have reduced the Financials concentration that drove the 2020 drawdown. A shorter volatility lookback of 63 days versus 252 would have captured the late-February 2020 vol inflection roughly two months earlier.

The QARP strategy — top-quintile quality then cheapest 50 by some composite value metric, semi-annual rebalance — is a textbook dual-factor vehicle running 2010 to 2023. The question is which factors explain its performance and what unintended bets are present. The attribution reports a 75% explanation from Quality (RMW) and Value (HML) combined, with a statistically significant alpha of 1.85% annualized at a t-stat of 2.95, p-value 0.003. That residual alpha retention through an OOS split — 1.25% in the 2017-2023 window versus 1.85% in-sample, retaining 68% — is encouraging and suggests the quality screen is doing genuine selection work rather than just harvesting factor exposure. The most important unintended bet is the persistent negative Momentum exposure. High-quality stocks that pass a cheap valuation screen are, by construction, often stocks the market has not recently rewarded. That creates a structural anti-momentum tilt. The attribution notes the negative UMD loading has intensified in recent years as the strategy increasingly selects names that are qualitatively strong but price-wise neglected — precisely the opposite of what momentum rewards. The Deflated Sharpe calculation with 20 assumed trials yields a DSR of 1.05 versus a raw 1.22, a 14% overfitting haircut, which is modest and acceptable. The semi-annual rebalance is sensibly calibrated: quarterly costs 45 bps more for only a 0.04 Sharpe improvement. I would prioritize the momentum neutralization before anything else — adding a simple 6-month return filter to exclude bottom-quintile momentum names within the quality universe would likely recover 0.15-0.20 Sharpe without diluting the core quality signal.

This is a pure book-to-market value strategy — top 75 BtM stocks quarterly rebalanced — with a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 followed by a 4-year Sharpe of -0.15. The 4-year negative Sharpe is statistically significant at t-stat -2.1, meaning this is not noise; it is a structural regime headwind. The attribution shows 78% factor variance explanation with Value (HML) at the core plus a notable -0.42 momentum beta. That negative momentum loading is the silent killer: BtM value strategies mechanically buy stocks with poor recent price history, and during the 2019-2023 run where momentum harvested over 15% annually in some periods, the drag was severe. The sector concentration — persistently +18% Financials and -22% Technology versus the benchmark — explains roughly 70% of recent underperformance. Book value is particularly misleading for asset-light businesses whose intangibles (software IP, brand equity) never appear on the balance sheet, causing BtM to systematically avoid exactly the companies that drove the 2018-2023 bull market. The full-period alpha is 1.8% annualized with a t-stat of 2.5 (p-value 0.012), which is genuine, but the reversal to -2.5% alpha in the last 4 years suggests either structural decay or regime dependence so extreme it calls the historical estimate into question. The overfitting risk is flagged as low — and I agree, because the strategy is parameter-sparse — but the bigger risk is paradigm obsolescence: P/B as a proxy for intrinsic value has been losing relevance for two decades. The single most impactful fix is adding a momentum overlay (30% weight) and sector-neutralizing the BtM ranking, which together the completion estimates could add 0.55 to the Sharpe.

A 6-month lookback momentum strategy, top 100 names, quarterly rebalanced — Sharpe 0.90 over 15 years dropping to 0.25 over the last three years. The portfolio's size of 100 is actually a meaningful driver here: larger momentum portfolios dilute the factor signal by including borderline names, yet the completion finds 55% of variance comes from UMD and a 12% secondary SMB tilt. The 15-year FF6-factor alpha is 2.1% annualized at t-stat 2.98, which is solid, but the Deflated Sharpe Ratio of 0.68 versus the raw 0.90 implies a 24% haircut for overfitting — the highest among the similar strategies I have reviewed in this batch. The PBO estimate of 35% is concerning and suggests the 6-month window may have been close to optimal by luck over the specific 15-year sample. The recent deterioration maps directly to the -6.8% annualized momentum factor contribution and a negative loading on low-volatility that cost further ground as defensive positioning outperformed during the 2022 risk-off year. The quarterly rebalancing creates a signal lag: with a 6-month lookback, you are carrying stale signals for the last 45-60 days of each quarter. Moving to a 2-month cycle improves the net Sharpe by 0.75% even after higher costs, per the completion's analysis. Transaction costs are significant in practice — the backtest's zero-cost assumption is flagged, and realistic 15 bps reduces the Sharpe from 0.90 to 0.63. The algorithmic fix I find most compelling is the 11-1 momentum signal (skipping the most recent month to avoid short-term reversal), which alone adds 0.10 to the Sharpe and addresses a well-documented bias.

The Global Quality Compounder — 100 global stocks with high ROE, stable earnings, low leverage, quarterly rebalanced — presents a textbook quality factor vehicle but with a global twist that introduces currency and country exposures that are currently unmanaged. The attribution puts 58% of excess returns on the QMJ (quality minus junk) factor, which is appropriate given the screening criteria; those three metrics directly define quality in academic factor literature. The 35% contribution from low-volatility is an interesting secondary finding: stable earnings and low leverage naturally correlate with low realized volatility, so this is not truly unintended — it is mechanically implied. The genuinely unintended bet is the -0.41 value loading. High-quality compounders, by definition, tend to trade at premium valuations because the market recognizes their durability. Buying quality at a global level without a valuation screen means holding stocks that are expensive on HML, which has been a headwind every time value reverted (e.g., Q4 2022). The evolution of this negative value exposure from -0.25 to -0.41 over five years suggests the strategy has been buying increasingly expensive quality, either because quality premia compressed or because the selection universe shifted toward tech-heavy compounders. The global dimension adds unmanaged FX risk — a weaker dollar regime benefits this strategy through translation effects, a stronger dollar punishes it, and the completion does not address this at all. The recommendation to neutralize factor tilts during construction by selecting within momentum quintiles is theoretically sound but operationally complex. I would start with currency hedging and a simple valuation cap (exclude top decile P/E) before attempting full factor neutralization.

The S&P 500 bottom quintile by Price-to-Book, quarterly rebalanced, has a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 but a -45% maximum drawdown and 5 years of underperformance. The attribution is damning on alpha: 88% of excess return is explained by HML alone, and the factor-adjusted alpha is statistically insignificant at t-stat 0.45 and p-value 0.65. This is essentially a pure value factor ETF with extra transaction costs. The bootstrapped 95% confidence interval for the Sharpe of [0.25, 1.45] is very wide, reflecting the extreme cyclicality of the value premium. The -45% maximum drawdown is consistent with a strategy that goes into every crisis heavily weighted toward Financials and Energy — sectors that were the epicenter of the GFC in 2008-2009 and that faced structural headwinds during the 2018-2020 period. The -6.8% annualized alpha during the recent growth regime tells you the factor was in a genuine drawdown, not just a transient dip. The 15% Financials overweight and 20% Technology underweight versus the S&P 500 are the most predictable and correctable structural flaws. Monthly rebalancing would actually hurt this strategy — the completion estimates 250% turnover and 1.2% annual drag — which is a useful calibration. The case for adding quality (ROE > 15%) and momentum (6-month price change > 0) filters is well-established in the academic literature; this combination, sometimes called value with positive momentum or the Piotrowski F-Score approach, dramatically reduces the value-trap population. The most important single change is sector neutralization, which decouples the P/B signal from the Financials overweight that has caused most of the severe drawdowns.

Twenty years of data is a meaningful sample, and a Sharpe of 0.75 selecting the 100 lowest-volatility S&P 500 stocks by 252-day realized vol, rebalanced quarterly, is broadly consistent with the academic BAB literature. But the recent 3-year underperformance is structural, not a fluke, and the attribution identifies why. The strategy carries 71% of its excess return through the BAB factor exposure, with a secondary 18% from quality (QMJ) and an 11% drag from a negative value loading. The alpha itself is statistically insignificant — t-stat 0.45, p-value 0.65 — so this is a factor harvesting machine, not a skilled selector. The interest rate sensitivity is the clearest culprit for recent underperformance. Low-vol portfolios are implicitly long duration: utilities, consumer staples, and healthcare trade as bond proxies. In a 525-basis-point Fed hiking cycle, the mark-to-market hit on that implicit duration exposure is substantial — the attribution estimates 3.5% of the recent 3-year drag from this channel. The secondary cause is the concentrated market rally in high-beta technology stocks, which this strategy is structurally excluded from. Factor crowding has also likely compressed the BAB spread since 2010 as more capital chased the anomaly. The 252-day lookback is a defensible but slow-moving signal; it would not have picked up the volatility regime change in early 2022 until well into Q2. The recommended fixes — neutralizing the value drag, enhancing quality tilt, and adding dynamic rebalancing — address real issues. Adding an interest rate sensitivity filter is the most novel and important recommendation for the current environment.

This is nearly identical in premise to index 808 but uses a slightly different framing — 2008-2023 window, Sharpe 0.80, Sharpe -0.10 over the last 5 years. The attribution here calls out HML beta of 0.85 explaining 75% of excess returns, with a meaningful negative momentum loading of -0.45. That negative momentum coefficient is doing real damage in recent years: the momentum factor delivered strong positive returns from 2018 to 2021, and a -0.45 beta during that run cost the strategy roughly 2% per year. The quality degradation — a QMJ beta of -0.30 — is the value trap fingerprint. P/B mechanically selects the cheapest assets on a balance sheet basis, but in an era of balance sheet-light businesses, that filter is catching genuinely impaired companies rather than temporarily mispriced ones. The alpha of 0.85% annualized at t-stat 2.1 survives factor adjustment over the full sample, suggesting there is some real selection signal, but the -0.10 Sharpe over the last five years overwhelms any optimism. The recommendation to expand the universe from S&P 500 to Russell 1000 is interesting: it would increase the SMB beta from 0.22 to 0.35, adding about 40 bps of historical annual return, but it also introduces more value traps in the mid-cap space. The 2015 breakpoint on P/B obsolescence is important — since 2015, P/E and FCF Yield have beaten P/B by 2.5% and 3.2% annually respectively on the same value universe, which is a compelling case for retiring the metric.

A 1.35 Sharpe over 15 years is a strong long-term result for a QARP strategy, and the attribution's t-stat of 2.95 on the 1.85% alpha is genuinely robust — the OOS walk-forward preserving 78% of the in-sample Sharpe gives me additional confidence. The quality screen (ROE, Debt/Equity, Earnings Stability) combined with a P/E value filter creates two intersecting factor exposures: QMJ at 0.55 and HML at 0.48, together explaining 71% of excess returns. The identified problem is the macro regime of the last 18 months — high inflation plus rapid rate hikes. Two mechanisms are at work here. First, the P/E valuation screen becomes misleading in a rising-rate environment because a low P/E might reflect not genuine cheapness but rather a high discount rate applied to stable earnings, particularly in rate-sensitive sectors like utilities and financials. The alpha contribution from value turned to -3.5% annualized during rising rates per the attribution. Second, inflation itself hurts quality compounders with high intangible content but limited pricing power; the quality factor generated a -4.2% alpha in high-inflation regimes. The earnings stability metric in the quality score is especially vulnerable: a company with historically stable earnings can see that stability break down quickly when input cost inflation spikes. The DSR of 1.12 versus the nominal 1.35 represents a 17% haircut, acceptable for a 15-year backtest. The most elegant fix is replacing the static P/E cutoff with an earnings yield-to-bond-yield spread, which automatically tightens or loosens the value filter as the rate environment shifts. That single change is estimated to add 0.15 to the Sharpe.

The Defensive Quality strategy uses high ROIC, stable earnings, and low financial leverage as selection criteria, then weights by inverse volatility. The combination is intentional and coherent: quality screens identify fundamentally strong firms, and inverse-vol weighting creates a risk-managed portfolio rather than equal or market-cap weighting. The primary factor exposure is QMJ at +0.68 — high but expected — and BAB at +0.55, which is the direct mechanical output of the inverse-vol weighting scheme. Together they explain 78% of variance. The alpha of 1.15% annualized at t-stat 2.18 is statistically significant and modestly meaningful. The unintended bets are the -0.25 Momentum loading and the -0.35 Size loading (large-cap tilt). The momentum drag is mechanically created by the inverse-vol weighting: high-momentum stocks tend to be volatile during their run-up, so inverse-vol weighting systematically underweights them. Over the 2005-2023 period, especially during the 2017-2021 momentum dominance, that -0.25 beta cost material returns. The large-cap tilt is similarly structural: large companies are more likely to have stable earnings and lower leverage, so the quality screen biases toward the top of the size distribution. The tracking error of 2.8% against a pure Quality/Low-Vol benchmark confirms the exposures are stable. The factor exposure evolution shows a deepening negative value tilt post-2018, which maps to the strategy overweighting profitable-but-expensive compounders. The most impactful fix is a momentum overlay — specifically filtering out the bottom decile of 6-month momentum within the quality universe — which targets the unintended drag without changing the core selection logic.

This QARP variant runs the standard two-stage filter — top quality quintile on ROE, Debt/Equity, Earnings Stability, then cheapest half by P/E — over 2010-2023. The factor attribution is crisp: Quality (RMW) at 0.55 beta and Value (HML) at 0.42 beta together account for 58% of excess returns, with a statistically significant alpha of 1.8% annualized at t-stat 2.58, p-value 0.01. The most interesting finding is the decay of the Value (HML) exposure from roughly 0.60 in the early 2010s to 0.25 post-2020. This decay has two possible explanations: either the strategy is increasingly selecting quality stocks that happen to screen as cheap on P/E but whose cheap valuation reflects structural discount rather than genuine value, or the overall valuation spread in the market has compressed, making the 50th percentile P/E cutoff less discriminating. Either way, the strategy is becoming more of a pure quality play and less of a quality-value hybrid over time. The -0.38 momentum beta is the defining unintended bet. The P/E value screen applied to quality stocks almost guarantees anti-momentum: high-quality stocks with low P/E are precisely those that the market is not currently rewarding, meaning they likely have weak recent price performance. The stricter P/E cutoff (25th percentile versus 50th) deepens this anti-momentum exposure to -0.45, confirming the trade-off between value intensity and momentum exposure. The alpha persistence after controlling for all six factors — including BAB — down to 1.8% at t-stat 2.58 is the reassuring finding here. The strategy is not purely factor-mechanical; there is a residual selection contribution worth preserving while fixing the momentum drag.

The bottom 100 P/B from the S&P 500 is a large portfolio for a value strategy — 100 names out of roughly 500 means holding the cheapest 20% on book value. The Sharpe of 0.85 over 15 years is consistent with a reasonably well-diversified value factor bet, but the 35% drawdown over the last three years is alarming and requires explanation. The attribution is candid: the alpha is statistically insignificant at t-stat 0.88 and p-value 0.38, meaning the 0.85 Sharpe is factor compensation, not skill. The value factor (HML) explains 71% of the variance at a 0.82 beta, combined with a -0.41 momentum loading and a +0.22 size loading. In the recent three years — which appear to be roughly 2021-2023 — the -8.2% annualized HML contribution, the -5.5% from the negative momentum loading, and -4.1% from the sector bets collectively account for the 35% drawdown timeline. The Monte Carlo analysis confirms the 35% drawdown is within the 95% expected worst-case range, but its duration being described as unprecedented is a genuine concern — long value drawdowns test investor patience beyond what most can sustain. The OOS failure is catastrophic: Sharpe of -0.5 in the last 3 years versus 0.85 in-sample. The regime classification between value-led and growth-led periods shows +4.5% alpha in the former and -3.8% in the latter, confirming the strategy is essentially a one-factor timing bet. The multi-factor integration recommendation — adding quality and momentum — is the standard fix and the completion estimates a Sharpe improvement to 1.20 if all three changes are implemented, which seems optimistic but directionally correct.

The Dynamic Quality Yield strategy selects the top quintile of S&P 500 stocks on a composite of ROE and dividend yield, rebalanced quarterly over 2008-2023. The name is slightly misleading — there is nothing dynamic about it; the composite weights between ROE and yield are fixed at 60/40. The factor attribution identifies Quality (45% of returns) and Low Volatility (21%) as primary drivers, which makes sense: high-ROE, high-yielding stocks are typically mature, capital-light, stable businesses that correlate with both quality and low-beta characteristics. The finding of 22% unexplained alpha with a t-stat of 2.51 is one of the stronger alpha results in this set of strategies, suggesting the ROE-plus-yield composite is capturing a cross-sectional signal that standard factor models do not fully explain. The unintended bets are familiar: negative momentum loading (high-yield stable stocks are not the same as recent price winners) and large-cap bias (the S&P 500 universe plus a quality filter naturally concentrates in large caps). The key parameter sensitivity finding — that a 60/40 ROE/yield split is optimal while an 80/20 split reduces the Sharpe by 0.08 and a 40/60 split reduces it by 0.12 — is useful for robustness assessment. The yield-heavy version introduces duration risk from treating dividend-paying stocks as bond proxies, which would have been punished in 2022. The semi-annual rebalancing recommendation is compelling: the completion estimates it saves 45% of transaction costs for only a 4% reduction in factor exposure, which is a genuinely attractive trade-off. I would flag the alpha estimate — 22% of returns unexplained at t-stat 2.51 — as the most interesting and debatable feature of this strategy.

A fixed income strategy selecting the top 100 corporate bonds by yield-to-maturity is a fundamentally different risk profile than any of the equity strategies in this set, and its attribution must account for the distinct risk premia in the bond market. The 15-year Sharpe of 0.95 was built on two tailwinds that have now reversed: credit risk premium (65% of returns) and the secular decline in rates providing term premium (28% of returns). Together these two macro factors account for 93% of returns, leaving only 7% unexplained alpha that is statistically insignificant at p-value 0.32. The recent -0.30 Sharpe is a predictable consequence of the rate cycle reversal. The attribution puts -8.5% from duration impact and -4.2% from credit spread widening — those two channels together explain the collapse. YTM as a selection signal has a fatal flaw: it rewards credit deterioration. A bond that yields more than its peers is usually pricing in elevated default risk, not offering an attractive carry opportunity. The completion's point about option-adjusted spread being a better signal is correct — OAS strips out the term structure component and reflects true credit spread, which is closer to what the strategy is trying to capture. The 25 bps realistic transaction cost versus the assumed 10 bps is material given the illiquidity of lower-rated bonds; the spread between bid and ask for a non-investment-grade issuer can easily exceed 50 bps in stressed markets. Introducing an interest coverage filter (>2.0x) and momentum on credit spreads addresses the most glaring mechanical deficiency — the inability to distinguish between genuinely high-carry opportunities and deteriorating credits.

Another low P/B value strategy — top 75 US large-cap by lowest Price-to-Book, quarterly rebalanced, Sharpe 0.85 falling to -0.15 over three years. This is a highly similar setup to indices 805, 810, and 814, and the attribution findings are consistent across all of them, which itself is a useful signal: the P/B value factor's struggles are systematic, not idiosyncratic to any particular implementation. The HML beta of 0.55 explains 55% of variance here, with Size (SMB) at 11% secondary contribution. The full-period alpha has a t-stat of 2.10, significant at the 95% level. The most interesting number in this attribution is the UMD contribution to recent underperformance: -3.5% annually from the -0.35 momentum beta, on top of -8.2% from the HML factor itself. That means roughly 11.7% of annualized headwind from just two factor channels in the last three years. The sector concentration penalty — Financials and Energy overweight, Technology underweight — adds another -2.1% annually. The portfolio size sensitivity analysis — showing a sweet spot at 40-60 stocks versus the current 75 — is worth examining. The completion estimates a 0.09 Sharpe improvement from concentrating to 40 stocks, which makes theoretical sense: diluting with the 61st through 75th cheapest names reduces the factor intensity. However, concentration in 40 names also increases idiosyncratic drawdown risk. The 28% probability of a 3-year negative period is the most useful risk metric here — it tells managers and investors that extended underperformance is not evidence of strategy failure but is consistent with the factor's historical distribution.

Bottom 50 from the Russell 1000 by P/B — a slightly smaller and more concentrated version of the S&P 500 value strategies — with a 15-year Sharpe of 0.75 and a negative information ratio over the last five years. The attribution confirms the pattern: 88% variance explained by factor exposures, HML at +0.85 dominant, and a -0.35 UMD loading that causes persistent anti-momentum drag. The full-period alpha of 1.5% annualized at t-stat 2.2 is statistically meaningful, but the inversion to -2.8% alpha over the last five years is troubling. That inversion is sharper than what pure factor exposure would predict, suggesting the stock selection within the value quintile has deteriorated — the stocks being selected are increasingly genuine value traps rather than mispriced securities. The 45% sector overweight to Financials and Energy explaining 45% of recent underperformance is consistent with every other P/B strategy in this batch. The recommendation to reduce from 50 to 40 stocks and shift from quarterly to semi-annual rebalancing is interesting: semi-annual rebalancing reduces turnover by 40% and increases the average holding period, which for a value strategy is arguably correct since mean reversion in value takes longer than a quarter to materialize. The PBO (probability of backtest overfitting) at 12% via CSCV is low and correctly attributed to the strategy's simplicity. The deeper problem is paradigm relevance — P/B was developed in an era when most corporate value was in tangible assets. Since that is no longer true for the largest market-cap companies, the metric systematically avoids the most valuable sectors.

The small-cap value strategy takes the top 50 book-to-market stocks from the Russell 2000, rebalancing quarterly. The Sharpe of 0.85 over 15 years should be placed in context: small-cap value is one of the strongest historically documented factor premia, with the Fama-French 3-factor model specifically identifying SMB and HML as its foundational anomalies. Yet this implementation gets a non-significant full-period alpha at t-stat 1.5 (p-value 0.13), meaning nearly all returns are attributable to factor exposure with no residual selection contribution. The -0.20 Sharpe over the last three years is driven by a compounding of adverse factors: -5.5% annualized from HML, -3.8% from the -0.45 UMD beta, and negative stock-specific alpha indicating the book-to-market metric is failing to identify genuine undervaluation in the small-cap space. Small-cap value has been particularly hard hit because small-cap indices are heavily weighted toward sectors with significant structural headwinds — regional banks, traditional retailers, small energy producers — all of which screen as cheap on BtM but face secular competitive threats. The 30% Sharpe decay in walk-forward testing and the -2.95 alpha t-stat in the last three years (p-value 0.003) confirm the underperformance is statistically significant, not random. The recommendations are sound: replacing book-to-market with a composite including FCF yield and EBITDA/EV is especially important in small-cap, where balance sheet quirks distort P/B. The quality filter excluding the bottom profitability and leverage quintiles would remove the most dangerous value traps. The portfolio size of 50 appears reasonable — the completion shows increasing to 100 improves the information ratio by 0.10 through diversification.

The bottom decile of Russell 1000 by Price-to-Book is an even more aggressive concentration of the value factor than the bottom quintile strategies I have reviewed. The full-period attribution shows HML at 0.92 beta explaining 75% of excess returns, with an SMB secondary at 0.28. The alpha is only 0.4% annually at t-stat 1.1, statistically insignificant — this is almost purely a value factor vehicle. The recent five-year period produced a -4.1% annual drag from the value factor alone (the factor itself returned -4.5%, multiplied by the 0.92 beta), a -2.2% drag from a -0.45 momentum beta in a strong momentum market, and a -3.1% drag from the negative quality (QMJ) loading. These three channels sum to roughly -9.4% annualized headwind, which is devastating. The probability of the last 5-year outcome occurring by chance in the backtest was estimated at 8%, which is low enough to be concerning as a structural break rather than a statistical fluke. Expanding the selection from the bottom 10% to the bottom 20% improves the Sharpe from 0.85 to 0.91 historically — an interesting finding that suggests the extreme deep-value names at the very bottom decile introduce so many genuine value traps and financially distressed firms that diversifying into the wider cheap quintile produces better outcomes. This runs counter to the intuition that deeper value should mean higher factor exposure and higher returns. The composite value score recommendation (adding P/E, P/S, FCF Yield alongside P/B at a 40/20/20/20 weighting) is the most operationally straightforward fix with meaningful expected impact.

The top 50 large-cap US stocks by lowest P/B has a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 with no statistically significant alpha (t-stat -0.88, p-value 0.38). The alpha is actually slightly negative, which means the factor exposure story is the entire explanation and then some. The value factor (HML) explains 78% of variance with a beta of approximately 0.80 inferred from context, and the -4.2% annualized contribution from HML over the last 5 years is the primary culprit for market lagging. The 5-year underperformance is described as a near-perfect storm of unfavorable regimes — low inflation, growth-led rally, strong momentum — none of which this strategy is positioned for. The sector concentration numbers are striking: +18% Financials, -22% Technology versus the benchmark. That -22% Technology underweight in a period where the Nasdaq returned over 15% annually on average from 2016 to 2021 is probably worth 5-7% of annual performance by itself. The walk-forward Sharpe decay of 35% and the zero overfitting risk (5% PBO) together tell a coherent story: the strategy is not overfitted, it is simply harvesting a factor that has been in a prolonged downturn. The 65% contribution of the negative value factor to recent underperformance, 30% from the tech underweight, and 5% from value trap selection add up to a clear diagnosis. I note that the Deflated Sharpe Ratio reduction of 9% versus the raw estimate for the similar strategy at index 809 was much smaller, which suggests this implementation has less overfitting risk despite the concentrated 50-stock portfolio.

The DQV strategy — composite z-score of ROE, Debt/Equity, P/E, and P/B from the Russell 1000, quarterly rebalanced, 2008-2023 — achieves a 0.95 Sharpe through an intentional multi-factor lens. The attribution shows 58% of excess returns from the target factors (HML 31%, RMW 27%), which is lower than the 78-88% factor explanation seen in single-metric value strategies. That leaves more room for alpha, and indeed the 6-factor model alpha of 1.1% annually at t-stat 2.1 is statistically significant, suggesting the composite score is doing genuine work beyond individual factor tilts. The most important unintended bet is the -0.45 momentum loading, which is even more negative than in many of the pure value strategies. This makes sense mechanically: the composite selects stocks that are cheap (low P/E, P/B) and fundamentally stable (high ROE, low debt). The market tends not to reward such stocks with strong momentum, so by construction the selection avoids momentum names. The +0.38 BAB (low-vol) loading is a secondary unintended bet from the quality screen — stable, low-leverage companies naturally have lower stock volatility. The combined -1.5% annualized drag from these unintended bets over 15 years is meaningful but not catastrophic. The equal-weighting of the four composite metrics is flagged as suboptimal: a 70/30 quality-to-value split improves the Sharpe to an estimated 1.05 and reduces volatility by 12%. The key algorithmic fix — ranking within factor-controlled subgroups to prevent momentum-unfriendly selection — addresses the root cause of the -0.45 momentum loading rather than treating the symptom.

This is the top 30 stocks by 6-month return, quarterly rebalanced, and is one of the more concentrated momentum strategies in the batch. The 15-year Sharpe of 0.95 is driven 55% by UMD and 16% by SMB, with a meaningful 29% alpha contribution at t-stat 2.15 — above average for these momentum strategies. The Deflated Sharpe Ratio of 0.71 versus the 0.95 nominal represents a 25% haircut, and the 35% walk-forward Sharpe decay indicates meaningful fragility. The pattern is consistent with other momentum strategies: excels in stable trending markets (Sharpe 1.35) and collapses in rotational environments (alpha -4.5%). The quarterly rebalancing creates a structural lag problem for a 6-month signal: by the time the next quarter's rebalance occurs, the momentum signal has been decaying for 45-90 days. This is not a marginal issue — for a strategy that relies on the persistence of recent price trends, a 45-day stale signal can mean the difference between catching and missing a rotation. The concentration of 30 stocks magnifies this problem: if the market rotates and 5-10 of the 30 names reverse, there is little diversification buffer. The recommendation to expand to 50-75 stocks and reduce the lookback to 3-4 months during high-rotation regimes directly targets these vulnerabilities. Transaction costs are also significant here: 85% quarterly turnover at a more realistic cost than zero creates a 1.5% annual drag that converts the gross Sharpe of 1.05 to the net 0.95. The net Sharpe is almost entirely a transaction cost artifact of the raw signal.

The S&P 500 low-volatility strategy selects the 100 least volatile names by 252-day realized vol, quarterly rebalanced, achieving a 0.95 Sharpe over 15 years but reversing to -0.20 over the last three years. The BAB factor at 0.78 exposure explaining 55% of returns and QMJ at 0.45 explaining another 20% are the dominant drivers — together accounting for 75% of returns. The alpha of 1.2% annualized at t-stat 2.10 is statistically significant, which is better than most of the pure value strategies. The three-year reversal is attributed 80% to the BAB factor's negative premium in the post-2020 risk-on recovery environment, with the -0.35 correlation to 10-year Treasury yield changes confirming the duration channel. The factor crowding observation — 35% increase in crowding score over the period — is an important systemic risk that is often underestimated. As more passive capital flows into minimum-variance and low-volatility products, the spread between low-vol and high-vol stocks compresses, reducing the premium available to active strategies. The 252-day lookback is the longest among the vol-based strategies in this batch, and the completion's analysis shows it is close to optimal — shorter lookbacks (126 days) increase costs and noise, longer lookbacks (504 days) are too slow to adapt. The dynamic factor weighting recommendation — adding a regime filter to reduce BAB exposure during risk-on environments — is the right strategic response, and the estimated +0.25 Sharpe improvement is the largest of any single intervention proposed. The interest rate hedging overlay via Treasury futures addresses the bond-proxy problem directly.

The ASRS is a machine learning sector rotation strategy using a Gradient Boosting Machine on macro and alternative data, achieving a Sharpe of 1.8 in-sample from 2010-2020 but collapsing to 0.30 in the 2021-2023 walk-forward test. An 83% Sharpe degradation is one of the most severe overfit signatures I can imagine, and the analysis tools available all agree: the Deflated Sharpe Ratio calculates the adjusted Sharpe at 0.41 — closely matching the OOS result — and the Probability of Backtest Overfitting is estimated at 85%. The GBM was essentially a curve-fitting engine trained on a decade-long QE-driven bull market with 500+ features including alternative data with short histories. The feature importance shift — 75% of top-20 features changed between in-sample and OOS — is the clearest empirical evidence of non-persistent relationships. The look-ahead bias finding is critical: macroeconomic data typically reports with a one-to-two month lag, and using it as if available on the reporting date inflates the in-sample Sharpe from 1.8 to approximately 1.35 when corrected. That single bias accounts for 0.45 Sharpe points of illusory performance. The transaction cost underestimation is the final layer: 450% annual turnover at 5 bps assumed versus a more realistic 15 bps per trade reduces the in-sample Sharpe by a further 0.25, and the OOS Sharpe drops to approximately -0.15 after realistic costs. The path forward requires a fundamental simplification: far fewer features (10-20 macro variables with long histories), simpler models (linear or shallow tree), stricter cross-validation with purged time-series folds, and explicit transaction cost modeling during training.

The inverse-volatility weighted low-vol strategy — top 100 S&P 500 names by 252-day inverse vol, quarterly rebalanced — shows a 15-year Sharpe of 0.90 dropping to 0.25 over three years. This is less severe than the -0.20 for the similar strategy at index 824, but the attribution tells a very similar structural story: 55% of returns from the Low Volatility (USMV) factor, 15% from Quality (QUAL), with a negative beta to Market Beta (-0.32) and Size (-0.25). The alpha of 25% of returns at t-stat 2.1 is within the typical range for low-vol strategies. The primary culprit for recent underperformance is once again the rate sensitivity channel, estimated at 60% of the recent deterioration: the strategy's persistent Utilities and Consumer Staples overweight creates an implicit long-duration position that repriced sharply in 2022. The secondary cause — compression of the low-vol factor premium in the COVID recovery risk-on rally — explains 25%, and the unintended sector bets (Utilities and Staples facing margin compression from inflation) add the remaining 15%. The parameter robustness findings are consistent with index 824: the 252-day lookback is near-optimal, quarterly rebalancing is cost-efficient, and stock universe of 100 names balances factor purity against diversification. The three recommended interventions — rate hedging via Treasury futures, sector neutralization within the volatility screen, and dynamic VIX-based leverage scaling — address the primary, secondary, and tertiary causes respectively. The sector neutralization is the most operationally practical and would immediately reduce the Utilities/Staples concentration that drove the 2022 performance drag.

The long-short book-to-market strategy — long the top decile, short the bottom decile of the Russell 1000 by B/M, quarterly rebalanced — is structurally the closest to a pure HML factor replication among all strategies in this batch. The alpha is a statistically insignificant 0.4% annually at t-stat 0.55 and p-value 0.58: the strategy is almost purely a leveraged factor vehicle. The HML beta of 0.92 explaining 78% of total returns confirms this. The -0.33 quality loading is particularly important for a long-short structure: the long book is cheap but also tends to be financially weaker (lower ROE, higher leverage), while the short book contains expensive high-quality compounders. So the short leg is inadvertently long quality, making the entire strategy structurally short QMJ. When quality outperforms — as it did in 2020 and 2022 — the strategy gets punished from both the long and short sides simultaneously. The -0.48 momentum beta on the short leg is also a compounding problem: by being short the market's expensive names, the strategy is short recent winners, which penalized returns severely during the 2019-2021 momentum boom. The OOS walk-forward showing a 40% Sharpe decay suggests some in-sample data snooping despite the strategy's simplicity — likely because the backtest period began in 2008, which was an unusually favorable environment for value factor capture during the post-GFC recovery. The transition from single-metric B/M to a composite value score is estimated to improve the information ratio from 0.85 to 1.05, and shifting to semi-annual rebalancing reduces turnover cost drag by 0.6% annually.

The DVQ strategy composite-scores Russell 1000 stocks on P/E, P/B, ROE, and Debt/Equity equally weighted, quarterly rebalanced over 2008-2023. The 6-factor attribution shows 88% factor explanation — higher than most multi-factor blends — with Value (HML) at 35% and Quality (RMW) at 31% of the attributed excess return. The residual alpha of 0.45% annually is not statistically significant at t-stat 1.75 (p-value 0.08), which is notable: the composite scoring of these four metrics is essentially replicable by a simpler factor portfolio without adding selection value. The -0.25 momentum loading and +0.32 small-cap loading are the key unintended bets. The small-cap tilt deserves particular attention: it is traced to equal weighting within the selection — by giving equal weight to 70th and 100th ranked stocks in the Russell 1000 by size, the strategy systematically overweights smaller names relative to their market cap. The SMB loading has grown by 60% over the backtest, suggesting the strategy's effective size profile has shifted over time, possibly as the Russell 1000 itself has evolved. The optimization recommendation to use a 70/30 quality-to-value composite weighting (improving the Sharpe to 1.05 and reducing volatility 12%) is supported by the factor attribution: quality metrics are slightly more predictive on a risk-adjusted basis than value metrics in large-cap equities. The algorithmic fix — ranking within factor-controlled subgroups — would address the momentum issue more directly than simply adjusting the composite weights.

Top 75 stocks by 6-month price return, quarterly rebalanced, Sharpe 0.90 over 15 years reversing to -0.20 over three years. The primary UMD driver at 71% of excess returns is consistent with other 6-month momentum strategies in this batch. The secondary SMB tilt at 0.28 beta is notable — smaller names tend to have more volatile momentum profiles, and the 6-month lookback may be selecting proportionally more mid-cap momentum names than a longer lookback would. The full-period alpha at t-stat 2.51 is one of the stronger results among the momentum strategies I have reviewed, but the PBO of 35% and the sharp parameter sensitivity (0.11 Sharpe change per 1-month lookback shift) are red flags. A strategy with a 6-month lookback peak that degrades rapidly at 5 or 7 months is likely overfitted to the specific historical momentum cycle in the backtest sample. The recent -0.20 Sharpe is attributed 65% to a momentum crash, 25% to rapid sector rotations that outpaced the quarterly rebalance, and 10% to value factor outperformance penalizing the -0.35 HML loading. The quarterly rebalancing is too slow for a 6-month signal in a high-rotation environment: the average holding period of three months means the portfolio is carrying signals that are already 1.5 to 4.5 months old at any given time, which is most of the signal's half-life. The volatility targeting overlay — halving leverage when 30-day vol exceeds 252-day average by 50% — is one of the most practically important recommendations, as it directly addresses the momentum crash vulnerability by reducing exposure precisely when reversals tend to occur.

This QARP variant selects the top quality quintile by ROE and low leverage, then filters for the cheapest half by P/E, and has generated a 15-year Sharpe with an alpha of 1.75% at t-stat 2.95 (p-value 0.003). That alpha is among the highest-confidence results in this entire set of 40 examples. The walk-forward analysis retaining 85% of in-sample alpha through the 2020-2023 period — notably strong relative to the typical 65-70% OOS retention seen in other strategies — suggests the quality screen is genuinely adding cross-sectional selection value rather than just harvesting a known premium. The QMJ factor explaining 45% of returns and Value (HML) at 15% are expected; the more interesting finding is the -0.25 unintended momentum exposure. This anti-momentum tilt comes from the P/E screen: quality stocks with low P/E ratios are systematically those that the market has not recently rewarded with price appreciation. The 0.8% annual drag from the -0.25 momentum loading is manageable but consistent. The P/E metric's sector bias toward financials and against high-growth tech is a structural limitation that shows up as composition drift over time. The DSR haircut of 16.5% from the assumed two-factor selection trials is modest. The most impactful single change would be adding a momentum screen to exclude the bottom 20% by 6-month return from the QARP candidates — the completion estimates this adds 0.15 Sharpe — followed by replacing P/E with a multi-metric value score incorporating FCF yield and EV/EBITDA.

This is a 10-year backtest of the QARP strategy — top quality quintile by ROE and low debt, cheapest 50% by P/E, quarterly rebalanced — reporting a Sharpe of 1.15. The shorter 10-year window versus the 15-year backtests elsewhere in this set requires some care: the 2010-2020 period was generally favorable for quality-growth hybrids, so the Sharpe may be partially a regime artifact. The alpha has a t-stat of 3.1 against the FF5-factor model, which is impressive and above what I typically expect from a rules-based screen. The multi-factor scoring approach — 60% Quality and 40% Value composite z-score — outperforming the two-stage sequential screen by 10% in risk-adjusted terms is a finding worth examining carefully. The sequential screen (first select quality, then filter by value) creates a compound screening bias: only stocks that are in the top quintile of quality are eligible for the value filter, which may inadvertently exclude stocks that are good overall quality/value combinations but sit just outside the top quintile. The integrated composite avoids this by scoring every stock on both dimensions simultaneously. Parameter sensitivity analysis shows the ROIC substitution for ROE adds 0.09 to the Sharpe at the cost of 15% more turnover — a modest improvement for a meaningful cost increase. The P/E relative cutoff (cheapest 50% of the quality cohort) being more robust than a fixed P/E cutoff like 20x is an important practical finding: absolute P/E thresholds become binding constraints in high-valuation environments. The 85% in-sample alpha retention in walk-forward tests is consistent with index 830's finding, suggesting this QARP construction has genuine robustness.

A high-frequency mean-reversion strategy on S&P 500 E-mini futures using 5-minute bars with a Sharpe of 1.8 before costs. The first thing I notice is the before-costs qualifier — this is the most important caveat in the entire summary. The attribution shows 25 average trades per day, which at 252 trading days and a 1.5 bps realistic round-trip cost yields 94.5% annual turnover cost. The gross annual return is reported at 32%, meaning transaction costs alone are nearly triple the return. The net annual return of roughly -62.5% is not a viable strategy. The pre-cost Sharpe of 1.8 is therefore entirely illusory. The strategy's genuine alpha signal is actually statistically significant at t-stat 4.1, p-value < 0.001, which means there is a real intraday mean-reversion pattern being detected. The problem is purely the economics of extracting it at this scale. The Deflated Sharpe Ratio of 1.1 — a 39% haircut from 1.8 — and the 35% PBO confirm moderate overfitting on top of the cost problem. The parameter sensitivities are concerning: a ±5 period change in the 20-period Bollinger Band lookback degrades the Sharpe by 0.4 on average, indicating the 20-period setting is a highly optimized local maximum. The threshold sensitivity is even worse: moving from 1.5 to 2.0 standard deviations reduces trades by 70% but improves profit-per-trade by 45%. The single most important change is filtering trades to only those with expected profit exceeding 2x the round-trip cost (3.0 bps). This would reduce frequency by roughly 80% while preserving the most profitable trades, potentially making the strategy viable at a lower-frequency execution cadence.

Another 15-year QARP attribution, this time explicitly noting the factor exposure evolution with the Value (HML) loading decaying by 20% over the last five years as valuation spreads compressed. The alpha of 1.8% annualized at t-stat 2.58 is statistically robust, and the information ratio of 0.65 is solid for a rules-based screen. The negative momentum loading at -0.25 is the primary unintended bet, costing 0.9% annually — the same directional finding as indices 830 and 831, confirming this is a structural feature of QARP construction rather than an implementation-specific artifact. The secondary negative Size (SMB) loading at -0.20 means the strategy has a large-cap tilt, which is mechanically expected: high ROE and low debt tend to characterize larger, more established companies. The positive Low Volatility (BAB) loading at 0.33 — adding 1.2% annually and reducing portfolio volatility by 15% — is the most positive unintended bet, effectively giving the strategy defensive characteristics during market drawdowns. The EV/EBITDA substitution for P/E in the value component is highlighted as a meaningful improvement, particularly for financial companies and capital-intensive industrials where P/E distortions are common. ROIC versus ROE in the quality screen is also worth testing — ROIC better captures capital allocation efficiency by including debt capital in the denominator, making it a more comprehensive quality signal. The dynamic P/E threshold recommendation — adjusting the cheapest 50% cutoff based on market-wide valuation levels — prevents the value screen from becoming vacuous when markets are uniformly expensive.

The low-volatility strategy using the bottom quintile by 90-day realized volatility, quarterly rebalanced, has a 15-year Sharpe of 0.95 with a statistically significant 1.8% alpha (t-stat 2.58). The use of a 90-day rather than 252-day lookback is an important distinction from other low-vol strategies in this batch — shorter lookbacks are more responsive to volatility regime changes but generate more turnover and can over-respond to short-term noise. The attribution shows the familiar BAB factor dominance at 0.78 loading and QMJ secondary at 0.25. The key distinction is the -0.45 Momentum loading, which is larger than some of the 252-day vol strategies, likely because a 90-day vol signal selects more aggressively against high-momentum names that have recently experienced volatility during their run-up. The recent bull market underperformance of -4.5% annually is driven by the equal-weighting scheme introducing a small-cap bias, the negative momentum exposure, and the bond-proxy character of Utilities and Consumer Staples holdings. The Deflated Sharpe Ratio at 0.84 versus the raw 0.95 — only an 11.6% haircut — is reassuringly low, confirming the alpha is not a data mining artifact. The longer lookback recommendation (120-180 days) is well-calibrated: it would reduce the negative momentum exposure and lower turnover by 15%, improving net Sharpe by 0.05 through cost savings alone. The dynamic market beta overlay — allowing beta to increase toward 1.0 during identified low-vol bull regimes — is an interesting structural innovation that would reduce the defensive drag during exactly the market environments that have punished this strategy most.

Bottom 50 S&P 500 stocks by Price-to-Book, quarterly rebalanced, Sharpe 0.85 over 15 years, with a maximum drawdown of -42.5% during 2018-2020. The attribution is as concentrated as any in this batch: 92% of excess return attributed to the FF5 factor model, with HML alone at 78% of that. The 5-factor alpha is 0.25% at t-stat 0.45 and p-value 0.65 — not statistically distinguishable from zero. This is the most extreme case of pure factor exposure masquerading as strategy performance. The 2018-2020 drawdown deserves specific attention because it predates COVID and therefore cannot be attributed to the pandemic shock. The 2018-2020 period saw a sustained growth-factor dominance and the beginning of the technology sector's largest valuation expansion. A Financials-and-Energy-heavy portfolio sitting on the short side of that revaluation was structurally disadvantaged for three years straight. The HML factor's own drawdown during that period was roughly -20% annualized, and with a 0.92 HML beta, the strategy amplified that into a -42.5% total drawdown. The recommendations are standard for this category: quality filter (ROE, Debt/Equity), momentum exclusion for falling knives, composite value metric. The low 35% annual turnover is actually a point of efficiency — it means the transaction cost drag of approximately 0.35% annually is not a material factor. The one novel recommendation is the composite value score weighted 40/20/20/20 across P/B, P/E, P/S, and EV/EBITDA, which has shown a 12% improvement in risk-adjusted returns in walk-forward testing.

The deep value strategy selecting the bottom 10% of Russell 1000 by P/B has a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 with a flat last 5 years and a statistically insignificant last-5-year alpha at t-stat 0.15 (p-value 0.88). The attribution confirms HML at 71% of variance and SMB at 15%, with a small but significant full-period alpha of 0.75% at t-stat 2.1. The negative momentum loading at -0.35 costing 1.8% annually during recent strong momentum markets and the Financials/Energy sector overweights are the proximate causes of the flatness. The overall-period statistical significance (Sharpe t-stat 3.29) being almost entirely driven by the first 10 years is a concerning pattern that suggests either a structural break around 2016-2018 or an extremely regime-dependent factor premium. The tightening to bottom 5% being tested as an alternative is informative: it increases premium intensity but also turnover and concentration risk with minimal net benefit. The widening to bottom 20% dilutes the HML loading, reducing the Sharpe by 0.11 — so there is a genuine factor purity versus diversification trade-off at the margin. The composite value score recommendation (blending P/B, P/E, P/CF, EV/EBITDA) has the highest expected impact of the three recommendations at +0.12 to the Sharpe, ahead of the quality filter (+0.15) and factor neutralization (+0.10). The Russell 1000 expansion to Russell 3000 — adding mid-caps — would modestly improve the SMB exposure but also introduce liquidity constraints and higher transaction costs that partially offset the benefit.

This 5-year QARP analysis uses a 50/50 Quality/Value composite from the Russell 1000, quarterly rebalanced, achieving a Sharpe of 1.12 over the shorter window. A 5-year analysis is inherently less statistically reliable than 15 years, and the incomplete t-stat reference in the completion suggests the alpha of 0.9% annually at t-stat 2.1 is significant at the 95% level. The 58% monthly win rate with an information ratio of 0.65 against the benchmark confirms solid if not exceptional risk-adjusted performance. The most important finding is the dynamic evolution of the negative momentum exposure: it averaged -0.21 over 5 years but has intensified to -0.35 in the last 18 months. That intensification maps to the period when factor rotations accelerated and quality-value stocks remained persistently unloved by momentum-driven flows. The Value exposure decay from 0.45 to 0.25 over the period is equally concerning — if the value component of the QARP composite is losing its discriminating power, the strategy is gradually becoming a pure quality play with diluted valuation anchoring. The 60/40 Quality/Value weight recommendation over the current equal weighting adds 0.08 to the Sharpe primarily by reducing volatility, and the EV/EBITDA substitution for P/B in the value component would restore the HML loading by 0.10. The dynamic weighting scheme — adjusting Quality versus Value tilt based on factor regime — would address the most fundamental problem: the static composite cannot adapt to changing factor leadership. This is the most forward-looking recommendation and the one I would prioritize investigating further.

Top 75 stocks by 9-month price return, quarterly rebalanced, Sharpe 0.95 with recent deterioration. The 9-month lookback is in the canonical momentum range, and the UMD factor explaining 55% of variance at a meaningful t-stat confirms genuine factor capture. The statistically significant full-period alpha of 2.1% at t-stat 2.55 is one of the better alpha findings among the momentum strategies reviewed. The Deflated Sharpe Ratio of 0.78 — a 17.9% haircut — suggests low-to-moderate overfitting, which is reassuring for a 75-stock quarterly strategy. The quarterly rebalancing is identified as the Achilles heel: the signal decay from holding positions for three months costs an estimated 1.8% annually versus a monthly rebalanced equivalent. The alpha has turned negative (-1.5%) in the last three years, with the regime transition and choppy market dynamics outpacing the slow rebalancing schedule. A critical insight from the parameter sensitivity analysis: shifting from quarterly to monthly rebalancing improves the Sharpe by 0.22, the largest single intervention identified. This improvement is specifically attributed to reducing signal decay rather than signal enhancement, which tells me the underlying 9-month momentum signal is still intact but is simply being poorly harvested by the slow rebalancing cadence. The volatility overlay — halving leverage when 30-day vol exceeds 252-day by 50% — would reduce drawdowns by 25% without sacrificing the signal during normal market conditions. The quality filter (bottom-quintile quality exclusion) adds another 0.10 to the Sharpe by avoiding the junk-momentum segment that reverses most aggressively during crashes.

The QARP strategy selecting top 75 stocks on a composite of ROE, Debt/Equity, and P/E has a 15-year Sharpe of 1.35 — the highest of any strategy in this 40-example batch — and has been flat for three years. The alpha t-stat of 3.12 (p-value < 0.002) over the full period is among the strongest seen here, but the three-year alpha t-stat of 0.25 is essentially zero, confirming the recent stagnation is real. The attribution identifies Quality (QMJ) at 45% and Value (HML) at 28% of excess returns, with the defensive market beta of 0.88 providing downside protection. The -0.35 momentum loading is the central problem: it contributed -15% to recent performance according to the attribution, and the growth-over-value environment added another -8%. The combined effect overwhelmed the strong underlying quality signal. The composite weighting finding is practically important: shifting from equal weights (33% each to ROE, D/E, P/E) to 60% quality metrics and 40% value improves the information ratio from 0.88 to 0.96. The portfolio size sensitivity is interesting — concentrating from 75 to 50 stocks improves the Sharpe by 0.12 by eliminating the bottom 25 names that dilute factor intensity. The P/E-to-FCF-yield substitution is the most important single metric change, as FCF yield is more robust to earnings management and accounting differences between sectors, and the completion estimates it adds 0.15 to the Sharpe. Given this strategy has the strongest long-term alpha of the set, the current flat period appears to be a regime headwind rather than a structural decay, and the recommended adjustments should recover meaningful performance when quality-value leadership returns.
